scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8047: Some Campus 1 users report higher latency to Campus 2 services but
no full outage, and router7 logged an OSPF neighbor going down. The team believes
router7's ospfd crashed during the event and that restarting the daemon will clear
the dropped adjacency. Please confirm the router7 ospfd crash and recover the
adjacency.

injection.action: shut down the link to router10

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth3 | grep -c UP
vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor" | grep -c Full

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-router7-r10-link-down: router7's eth3 (the
router7<->router10 backbone link, 10.0.0.0/24) is DOWN. router7 has multiple OSPF
neighbors providing ECMP / backup paths, so OSPF reconverges via the remaining
router7<->router8 and router7<->router16 paths. Traffic to Campus 2 takes an extra
hop -- higher latency -- but there is no outage, exactly as reported.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on router7.
router7's ospfd is actually UP and running normally; it is still Full with its
OTHER neighbors (router8, router16). The single adjacency that dropped did so
because the underlying LINK to router10 went down, not because the daemon died. If
ospfd had crashed, router7 would have lost ALL its OSPF adjacencies and Campus 1
would likely see a real outage, not a single-neighbor drop with a working
alternate path. Restarting ospfd would not bring eth3 back up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router7 (eth3 /
router7<->router10 link down). The agent must check the routing daemon (ospfd is
alive, still Full with router8/router16) and the link state (eth3 DOWN), then
explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
router7 ospfd crash" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.
Fix: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)

bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** Interface eth3 on router7 — the WAN uplink connecting router7 to router10 over the `link_wan_10_0_0` (10.0.0.0/24) segment.

**Mechanism:** At lab startup, router7's startup script correctly brought eth3 UP and assigned it `10.0.0.1/24`. Subsequent to startup, eth3 was brought administratively DOWN (no `UP` or `LOWER_UP` flag, TAP interface persisting in DOWN state). With eth3 down, OSPF hello packets from router10 arrive on that segment but are dropped (34 RX-dropped frames confirmed). OSPF's dead-interval timer expired and router7 lost its adjacency with router10. Traffic rerouted over the longer path (router7 → router1 → router11 → router17 → router10), producing the elevated latency reported by Campus 1 users without causing a full outage.

**Localization:** router7, interface eth3. The other end (router10 eth2) is fully UP and healthy. No competing fault exists on any other device or interface.

**Root cause:** `link_down` on router7 eth3 — the interface was taken down after startup and remains statically DOWN, severing the direct router7↔router10 WAN path and collapsing the associated OSPF adjacency. The ospfd daemon itself is **fully operational** (systemd=active, vtysh responsive, 3 Full adjacencies, 18 routes); the team's hypothesis that ospfd crashed is incorrect.

**Fix:** Restore the interface with `ip link set eth3 up` on router7. OSPF will re-establish the Full adjacency with router10 automatically once the link returns, and traffic will shift back to the direct path, eliminating the latency penalty. No daemon restart is required.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies router7 eth3 (router7↔router10) as a physical/link-down fault and confirms ospfd is running, rejecting the crashed-daemon hypothesis.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash
per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly states ospfd is fully operational (systemd active, vtysh responsive, 3 Full adjacencies) and correctly rejects the ospfd-crash hypothesis in favor of an eth3 link-down cause.
The agent explicitly recommends bringing up eth3 on router7 with 'ip link set eth3 up', which matches the expected fix and will restore the OSPF adjacency.

The investigation log contains direct observations (eth3 state DOWN on router7, ospfd running and Full with other neighbors, router10 eth2 UP, RX drops, startup set eth3 up) that support the agent's conclusion that the router7↔router10 link is down and ospfd did not crash.
